questions.question: Describe Young and Willmott's symmetrical family and evaluate whether it accurately represents modern family life.
questions.correctAnswer: Young and Willmott: the family is becoming more equal - shared tasks, leisure and decision-making. Three stages led to symmetry: industrialisation, women working, technology. questions.question: Explain how feminism has challenged traditional family roles, using evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: Feminism challenged: the housewife role is socially constructed, not natural (Oakley); the family exploits women through unpaid labour (Delphy and Leonard); domestic violence is hidden behind 'private' family walls. Evidence: women do 60%+ of housework even when working full-time; the gender pay gap means women often earn less, reinforcing economic dependence.

questions.question: Evaluate whether conjugal roles have become more equal in modern families.
questions.correctAnswer: Evidence for greater equality: more dual-earner couples, men do more childcare than in the 1950s, some couples share tasks equally. Evidence against: women still do majority of housework, the dual burden, men control major decisions, commercialisation of housework (ready meals) masks ongoing inequality. questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the view that conjugal roles have become more equal in modern society. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: A grade 9 response will: describe Young and Willmott's symmetrical family; present Oakley's critique with evidence; discuss the impact of women's employment (dual burden); evaluate using recent evidence (BSA statistics); consider decision-making and money management; conclude: conjugal roles have become more equal than in the 1950s but full equality has not been achieved. Progress is uneven - some couples are more equal than others, and structural factors (gender pay gap, workplace culture) continue to disadvantage women in both public and private spheres.
